title: Equivalence partitioning: testing by categories
summary: The core black-box technique: split inputs into behaviour categories, write one case per category, and handle error categories and corner cases.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Equivalence partitioning (EP) is the first black-box test design technique. It rests on two assumptions: the production code does different things for different categories of input data, and if one value in a category works, every value in that category should work. Both are guesswork rather than guarantees, but they turn an infinite input space into a small, principled set of test cases.
The method is simple: read the specification, identify the categories of behaviour, write one test case per category, then choose test data and an expected result for each case.

sections.heading: Worked examples
paras: The sign function takes a real number and returns -1, 0 or 1 depending on whether it is negative, zero or positive: three categories, three cases. The absolute-value function has two categories (negative versus non-negative), and the palindrome check has two (reads the same forwards and backwards versus not). With several inputs, consider combinations: findMax(value1, value2) has three categories, value1 < value2, value1 = value2, and value1 > value2, not just each parameter in isolation.

sections.heading: Error categories
paras: Real submodules must also handle invalid input gracefully, and you must test that they do, even though bad input is the caller's fault. The formatTime submodule converts hours and minutes to HH:MM but must return error when either value is invalid. There is not one single invalid category: each parameter can be too low or too high independently, and the checks may be coded separately. Testing every combination gives eight error cases plus one valid case, nine in total: each of hours and minutes too low, in range, or too high, in every combination.
The lesson generalises: ask how many distinct ways the unit can reject input, and cover each one, because a bug in any single check slips through otherwise.

sections.heading: Rules that keep categories honest
paras: Write categories as plain ranges over numbers, smallest to largest, using only < and the non-strict variant, for example 0 <= x < 24. For strings and arrays, remember the corner cases people forget: the empty string and null (non-existence is not the same as emptiness). Zero is the classic corner case for numbers.

Four properties keep a category set valid. It must be complete: every possible input, including every combination for multi-parameter units, fits somewhere. It must contain no OR: a category like x < 0 or x >= 100 hides a test case. It must not overlap: no input belongs to two categories, so never write separate x < 0 and y < 0 categories for a two-parameter unit. And it must never test syntax errors: passing a string where a real is required is pointless because the compiler already prevents it.
bullets: Complete: every input (every combination) fits in exactly the intent of one category.
No OR: split x < 0 or x >= 100 into two categories so both get tested.
Mutually exclusive: x < 0 versus 0 <= x < 100, never x < 0 versus x < 100.
Corner cases: empty string, null, and zero get their own thought, not an afterthought.

callout.text: When asked to critique categories, run the four-property checklist: complete, no OR, no overlap, no syntax-error tests. For formatTime-style questions, enumerate all 9 cases; examiners award marks per missing error combination.

recall.q: What are the two assumptions behind equivalence partitioning?
recall.a: Production does different things for different input categories, and if one value in a category works, all values in it should work. Both are informed guesses, which is why EP is a starting point, not a proof.

recall.q: Why does formatTime need 9 test cases instead of 2?
recall.a: Because each of hours and minutes can be too low, in range, or too high independently (3x3 = 9 combos). One valid plus eight error cases, since each invalid combination may hide its own bug.

recall.q: Name the four properties of a valid category set.
recall.a: Complete (every input fits), no OR (each alternative is its own category), mutually exclusive (no overlaps), and no syntax-error tests (do not test what the compiler already forbids).

citations.excerpt: Write numeric categories smallest to largest using only < forms. Corner cases such as the empty string, null and zero are easily overlooked. Categories must be complete, contain no OR, not overlap, and never test syntax errors.

activities.prompt: Put the EP recipe in order.
activities.instructions: Drag the rows into the correct sequence.
activities.explanation: Understand, categorise, cover each category once, then concretise with data and expected results.

activities.prompt: The categories x < 0 and x < 100 are proposed for one input. What is wrong?
options: They overlap: some inputs fit both

distractor.1: There is no OR keyword; the problem is overlap.
distractor.2: Both are numeric ranges, not syntax tests.
distractor.3: Completeness is not the issue; mutual exclusion is.

activities.explanation: x = -5 fits both categories, so failures cannot be attributed. Rewrite as x < 0 versus 0 <= x < 100.

visuals.title: The EP recipe in four steps
visuals.what: From specification sentence to executable cases without drowning in values.
visuals.caption: One category, one case: that discipline is the whole technique.
visuals.alt: Four ordered steps for equivalence partitioning.

steps.title: Read the spec
steps.text: Find what the unit must do differently for different inputs.

steps.title: Name categories
steps.text: Write them as ranges (0 <= x < 24); include error categories.

steps.title: One case each
steps.text: Check completeness, no OR, no overlap, no syntax tests.

steps.title: Data + expected
steps.text: Choose concrete inputs and calculate each expected result.
